title: Terumah: gold inside and out (Exodus 25:11)
hookLine: the ark is gilded inside and out; the Talmud says a scholar's inside must match his outside (Yoma 72b)
tomorrow: Terumah: the cherubim face each other (Exodus 25:20–22)

cards: Some kitchens have a drawer like this. The front of it is lovely: painted wood, a brass handle. Pull it open and it's chaos: rubber bands, dead batteries, a key nobody can identify.
People can be a bit like that drawer, a polished outside and a different story inside. The first thing the Torah describes in the sanctuary plans isn't a wall or an altar.
It's a box: the ark that will hold the tablets of the covenant. And the instructions for gilding it are oddly specific about the inside.

teach.h: WITHIN AND WITHOUT SHALT THOU OVERLAY IT.
teach.b: The ark is made of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long. Then the instruction, in the old Jewish translation: "within and without shalt thou overlay it." Gold on the outside, which people might glimpse.
Gold on the inside, which almost no one would ever see. The tablets would sit in there, and the ark would stand in the holiest room, where, tradition says, only the high priest entered, once a year.
So why gild the inside? The Talmud gives a picture.
Betzalel, the craftsman, made three boxes, it says: a gold one, a wooden one, and another gold one. The wooden box sat inside the outer gold, and the inner gold sat inside the wood. Gold, wood, gold.
Then Rava, a sage of Babylonia, draws the lesson: any scholar whose inside is not like his outside is not a true scholar.

In Hebrew, tocho k'baro, his inside like his outside. Elsewhere the Talmud remembers Rabban Gamliel, head of the academy, who barred from the study hall any student whose inside did not match his outside.
Notice the ark isn't solid gold.
There's wood in the middle: ordinary, living material. Nobody is asked to be pure metal all the way through.
The ask is simpler, and harder: be the same inside as you appear outside. Don't polish only the side people see.

how: Tocho k'baro, inside like outside, is a phrase in Jewish ethical teaching about integrity, and the ark's gold within and without is cited for it in sermons on Terumah.

games.q: you're Betzalel, building the ark. the inside will hold the tablets, and almost no one will see it. what do you do with the inside?
o: leave it plain wood; who will know?
overlay it with gold, like the outside.
paint it to look like gold.
games.why: within and without shalt thou overlay it. the Talmud pictures gold, wood, gold, and draws the lesson: inside like outside.

practice: Notice one place where your outside and inside don't match right now: calm at work and frayed underneath, generous on the surface and resentful inside, saying you're fine. Don't judge the gap; just see it honestly.
Then ask what one small step toward matching might be, a true word to one person, or quiet inside work no one will see.

wordCard.voice: Terumah. Our portion, where the ark is overlaid with gold inside and out, and the Talmud says a scholar's inside must match the outside.
